newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian T-bill yields in new range - dealers.
newsitem.headline: Russian T-bill yields in new range - dealers.

text.p: Thursday's drop in Treasury bill yields to record lows on record high turnover was not a one-off development but marks the start of a new range, with Russian banks and enterprises increasingly happy to hold rouble instruments, dealers said on Friday.

The average yield, which fell to 26.1 percent on Thursday and was unchanged at that level on Friday, could fall further to 20 percent by the end of the year, even though prices may back down occasionally in the meantime, they said.
"I am not inclined to see this as a one-off price rise, the bounce back will be a small one," said Yevrofinans head of capital markets Alexei Rybnikov.
"It is obvious that we shall see a 20 percent annual yield by the end of the year, which means under an inflation rate of 10-11 percent banks will earn nine to 10 percent."

The previous sharp fall in yields on high turnover occurred in late February and early March, when the average yield fell to 24 percent on a mass inflow of non-resident funds, Central Bank figures show.
But as the volume of foreign investment eased off yields rose to 33-34 percent annual within two weeks.

The Central Bank said turnover on Thursday was 9.21 trillion roubles, compared to 6.44 billion roubles on February 27 and 8.41 trillion roubles on March 13, the previous record. The Moscow Interbank Currency Exchange (MICEX), the main trading centre, which counts turnover differently, said Thursday volumes were 8.54 trillion roubles, falling to 5.79 trillion on Friday.

"Everyone wants to believe prices will fall, and I think the drop in yields may stop, but not for a long time," a dealer said. "There is a potential for price growth in long-term paper due to non-residents' interests. Russia is still attractive compared to other emerging markets."
The current situation is akin to de-dollarisation, with companies increasingly willing to hold roubles rather than dollars, dealers said.
"The rouble is starting to gain weight not only in foreigners' eyes, but in the eyes of Russians," said CS First Boston head of fixed income Sergei Koshelenko.
"We are entering new levels by yields in all sectors of the market. The money inflow into the country is growing. For a while I see 20 percent as a benchmark for foreigners."

Interbank credits were cheap, with overnight credits falling to 1-5 percent on Friday, and roubles in plentiful supply. At the same time demand for dollars is not growing and the only place to park excess funds is the government securities market, pushing down yields, they said.
At the same time the equities market, itself hitting record levels, is not liquid enough to be a real alternative to the government securities market.
"The stock market in its current form does not suit banks, in its liquidity or in its volatility," Rybnikov said."
